solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Regularly connected in times gone by (4)

indicatorNotes.Regularly: take letters at regular intervals: every second one

blocks.note: the even letters of cOnNeCtEd

annotation.surface: Someone recalls being in regular touch with a friend in the old days.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' reads as how often you were in touch, but it tells you to pick every other letter of the next word.
annotation.definitionFit: Once is an adverb meaning formerly, at some time in the past, which is what 'in times gone by' says.

entries.clue: Arrest local in beauty salon (4,3)

blocks.note: to nail a criminal is informal for arresting them
your local is your neighbourhood pub, a bar

annotation.surface: Police arrest a local person in a beauty salon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Local' looks like a resident; in British use your local is the pub you drink at nearest home.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is a general category and the answer one kind of it: a salon given over to manicures.

entries.clue: Cardinal’s importance initially ignored (5)

indicatorNotes.initially ignored: the first letter is left out

blocks.note: weight is importance or influence
WEIGHT without its first letter W

annotation.surface: A cardinal of the Church finds his importance ignored at first.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' suggests a churchman, but here it is a cardinal number, a counting number like eight.
annotation.definitionFit: Eight is a cardinal number, as opposed to the ordinal eighth, so this is definition by example.

entries.clue: Senior officers stop bars becoming anarchic (3,5)

indicatorNotes.becoming anarchic: letters thrown into disorder are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: The generals want to close the bars before things turn lawless.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bars becoming anarchic' reads as pubs getting rowdy, but the anarchy is the letters of STOP BARS running riot.
annotation.definitionFit: Top brass is an informal idiom for the highest-ranking officers, from the gold braid on their uniforms.

entries.clue: Briefly sound one’s horn as well (3)

indicatorNotes.Briefly: cut short: the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: to toot is to sound a horn
TOOT without its last letter

annotation.surface: A driver gives a quick blast of the horn too.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' looks like a short honk, but it shortens the word itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Too is a plain synonym for as well, in the sense of also or in addition.

entries.clue: Popular investment product for the young? (5,4)

annotation.definition: Popular investment product for the young?

blocks.note: the surface says a best-selling savings account or fund; literally, the everyday place money is put away
the surface says a junior savings scheme; literally, the pig-shaped money box a child drops coins into

annotation.surface: A bank advert for a savings product aimed at young savers.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like a real financial product; the question mark flags that it is a child's money box, where many children first save.
annotation.definitionFit: A piggy bank is a pig-shaped money box, and it is where most children make their first investment.

entries.clue: Soldier who’s often found in same pub? (7)

annotation.definition2: who’s often found in same pub

blocks.note: a member of the permanent army rather than a reservist

blocks.clueFragment: who’s often found in same pub
blocks.note: a customer who keeps coming back to the same place

annotation.surface: A soldier who can usually be found propping up the bar at the same pub.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one person, but it is two senses of one word: a professional soldier and a habitual customer.
annotation.definitionFit: Regular is the noun for a full-time professional soldier, and also for a habitual customer of a pub or shop.

entries.clue: They help one see tiny particles, I’m told (5)

indicatorNotes.I’m told: what I hear: the word is heard, not spelt

blocks.note: specks are tiny particles

annotation.surface: Glasses that let you see tiny particles, or so someone says.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I'm told' flags a word you hear: specks of dust and specs on your nose sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: Specs is informal short for spectacles, and the definition describes what glasses do rather than naming them.

entries.clue: Noise made by the Bells in heated argument (4-4)

blocks.note: the sound of a ringing bell
British slang for a noisy row or fight

annotation.surface: The Bells, a family or a band, are making a racket during a fierce row.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Bells' makes them sound like people; a ding-dong is also British slang for a heated argument.
annotation.definitionFit: Ding-dong imitates the sound bells make, and British slang borrows it for a noisy row.

entries.clue: FBI agents — good chaps (1-3)

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
chaps are men

annotation.surface: Someone vouches that the FBI agents are decent fellows.
annotation.walkthrough: The (1-3) enumeration splits the answer as G + MEN, a hint that the first piece is a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: G-men, short for government men, is American slang for FBI agents.

entries.clue: Help a speculative venture (4)

blocks.note: used as it stands
a wager, a gamble on an outcome

annotation.surface: Someone asks for backing for a risky scheme.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Help' as a plea for support, but it is the definition, and the rest is A plus a gamble.
annotation.definitionFit: Abet is a narrower synonym of help: to assist or encourage, usually someone doing wrong.

entries.clue: Fan of The Crown? (8)

blocks.note: a supporter or devotee
the capitals suggest the Netflix drama about the Queen; literally, the Crown is the monarchy itself

annotation.surface: A viewer who loves the Netflix drama The Crown.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals point to the television series; the crown here is the monarchy, whose supporters are royalists.
annotation.definitionFit: The Crown is a standard name for the monarchy, and a royalist is someone who supports it.

entries.clue: Lifelike articles I manufactured (9)

indicatorNotes.manufactured: something made from raw material: the letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A craftsman boasts of the lifelike items he made.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Manufactured' pretends the articles were made in a factory; it is the instruction to rebuild ARTICLES I.
annotation.definitionFit: Realistic is a plain synonym of lifelike when said of a picture or model that looks true to life.

entries.clue: Fleet of ships near Madagascar is closing in (6)

indicatorNotes.is closing in: the answer is enclosed within the words before it

blocks.note: neAR MADAgascar

annotation.surface: A naval fleet off Madagascar draws ever closer.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the gap between two words; the surface fleet fits the definition so well that it hides the letters in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: Armada is a straight synonym for a fleet of warships, most famously the Spanish Armada of 1588.

entries.clue: OK to declare how old one is? (7)

blocks.note: to aver is to declare
your age is how old you are

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether it is all right to state their age.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface asks for permission, but 'OK' is an adjective here: middling, so-so.
annotation.definitionFit: Average can mean merely OK, neither good nor bad, a slightly grudging synonym.

entries.clue: Angry following American from one side to the other (6)

annotation.definition: from one side to the other

indicatorNotes.following: the first piece comes after the second

blocks.note: A is the usual abbreviation for American
cross means angry

annotation.surface: An irate figure pursues an American all the way over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following' means the angry piece comes after A, not that someone is being followed.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is a phrase paraphrasing the adverb: spanning a space from edge to edge.

entries.clue: Son harbouring desire to be a medic (7)

indicatorNotes.harbouring: sheltering something inside: one piece holds the other

blocks.note: used as it stands
an urge is a desire

annotation.surface: A boy nurses an ambition to become a doctor.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a boy's career ambition; 'Son' is not shortened to S here but kept whole and split open around the desire.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is a general category and the answer one kind of it: a medic who operates.

entries.clue: Heck, I’m so desperately longing to be back in Britain? (8)

annotation.definition: longing to be back in Britain?

indicatorNotes.desperately: in a frantic, wild way: the letters are thrown about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A Briton abroad exclaims how much they miss home.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: Britain is home only for a Briton.
annotation.definitionFit: Homesick means longing to be back home, which for a Briton is Britain, so this is definition by example.

entries.clue: Books acquired by old age pensioner freely available (2,3)

indicatorNotes.acquired by: taken in by: the second piece holds the first

blocks.note: OAP is the British abbreviation for old age pensioner
NT is the New Testament, the usual crossword books

annotation.surface: A pensioner picks up books that are being given away.
annotation.walkthrough: NT, the New Testament, is the usual crossword source of 'books'; an OAP is a retired person drawing the British state pension.
annotation.definitionFit: On tap is an idiom from beer drawn straight from the barrel, meaning available whenever wanted.

entries.clue: Mess about in large vessel (4)

blocks.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
Noah's ark is a vessel

annotation.surface: People fool around aboard a big ship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' could be a jug or a pot; here it is Noah's boat.
annotation.definitionFit: Lark is an informal British verb, usually 'lark about', for fooling around playfully.

entries.clue: Boys drinking nothing — or a lot? (5)

indicatorNotes.drinking: taking something in: one piece swallows the other

blocks.note: lads are boys
O looks like zero, nothing

annotation.surface: Do the lads drink nothing, or do they drink heavily?
annotation.walkthrough: The surface contrasts sobriety with excess; 'or' only joins the wordplay to the definition, 'a lot'.
annotation.definitionFit: Loads is an informal noun for a large quantity, the same as the definition's 'a lot'.

entries.clue: English social worker heading west for Italian hotspot (4)

indicatorNotes.heading west: in an across clue, west is leftward: the piece is written backwards

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
ants live in colonies and are the classic worker
reversal indicator: in an across answer, west is leftward, so the second piece is read backwards

annotation.surface: An English social worker travels to a sunny Italian destination.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' looks like a job title, but it is an ant, a social insect.
annotation.definitionFit: Etna is the active volcano in Sicily, literally a hot spot in Italy.

entries.clue: 13-year-old maybe knocking over green tea (8)

indicatorNotes.knocking over: upsetting something: the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A clumsy young teen spills a cup of green tea.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knocking over' sounds like a spilt cup, which suits the tea, but it rearranges GREEN TEA.
annotation.definitionFit: A 13-year-old is one example of a teenager, hence 'maybe'.

entries.clue: Take in Cockney’s warmth (3)

indicatorNotes.Cockney’s: Cockneys famously drop their H's, so the H goes

blocks.note: heat is warmth
HEAT without the H

annotation.surface: A Londoner absorbing the heat.
annotation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner whose accent drops the H, so 'eat' is how a Cockney says heat.
annotation.definitionFit: Taking in food is eating it, so the phrasal verb and the answer are straight synonyms.

entries.clue: Amphetamine discontinued? That’s a blow (8)

blocks.note: an upper is a stimulant drug
something discontinued has been cut

annotation.surface: Someone laments that their favourite stimulant has been withdrawn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That's a blow' sounds like a sigh of disappointment, but the blow is a punch.
annotation.definitionFit: An uppercut is one kind of blow, an upward punch in boxing, so the definition is the wider category.

entries.clue: Post small object (4)

blocks.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
an end is an object or aim

annotation.surface: Mail a little item.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a thing to post, but it means an aim, as in the end in view.
annotation.definitionFit: Post is a verb here, the British word for mailing a letter, and mailing something is sending it.
